source.title: PlatonicNav: Unveiling Semantic Correspondence in Navigation with Platonic Topological Maps
source.authors: Junlin Long; Ze-Yu Zhang; Xuren Deng; Yi-Ran Wang; Yue Yang; L. Borgnolo; Maxwell Twelftree; Yang Zhao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies blind matching between independently pretrained visual and language encoders, then evaluates language-goal navigation without paired vision-language data. This is a conceptual test of cross-model correspondence in an embodied setting, not a direct reproduction of the original representation-similarity measurement.
record.gate_note: The study reports navigation outcomes after blind matching, which bear indirectly on whether representations can be related without paired data. Its qualitative trajectory comparisons are not numerical representation-alignment measures. The HM3D-IIN results use a ground-truth visual goal mask and do not test cross-modal matching; the distance-metric, edge-weight, and segmentation ablations likewise do not test cross-model convergence.
record.test_reason: The study uses blind matching (DINOv3 vs GTR-T5) as a component of a navigation pipeline and reports only that pipeline's navigation scores (SR and SPL) against other navigation methods. It reports no matching accuracy and no mapping loss. It has no random-assignment or paired-supervision ablation of its own pipeline that would isolate the cross-modal correspondence. The navigation scores therefore cannot show whether the representations align or map onto each other with little loss. The authors call OVON results 'direct evidence', but the measure is the method's downstream performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that independently trained visual and language encoders share enough relational structure for blind matching to ground language goals in a vision-built map without cross-modal training. They present the OVON results as 'direct evidence' that the Platonic Representation Hypothesis carries over to navigation. They give no matching-accuracy evidence for that claim.
record.recipe_differences: The paper operationalizes the hypothesis in navigation using cluster-level pairwise distances and blind matching, then evaluates downstream task outcomes. It does not report the original-style direct comparison of normalized representation-distance matrices as its experimental outcome.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across navigation benchmarks and OVON splits; the paper does not compare alternative cross-modal alignment metrics or matching settings.

fits_no_version.finding: A training-free navigation pipeline that grounds language goals by blind matching DINOv3 and GTR-T5 embeddings reaches 48.7–51.8% success on HM3D-OVON (short-horizon subsets) and 63.5% on an R2R-CE subset. These numbers exceed several baselines trained with paired vision-language data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relational structure shared by independently trained vision and language encoders is enough to support downstream embodied goal grounding without paired data (a downstream-utility claim, not a measure of alignment).

record.problems: Cross-modal correspondence is supported indirectly through downstream navigation scores rather than a direct alignment or mapping-loss measure. The study uses one visual-language encoder setup and does not test scale, capability, multiple seeds, or alternative representation-similarity measures. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. HM3D-IIN results and the metric, edge-weight, and segmentation ablations were left out because they do not test cross-modal representation correspondence.

untested.parts: Blind-matching accuracy between DINOv3 cluster centroids and GTR-T5 category embeddings, mapping loss, comparison with paired or supervised grounding inside the same pipeline, and a chance-level control are all not reported.
No measure of image-caption alignment and no variation of model quality.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V4 'supports' label are overturned. Only navigation outcomes of the study's own method are reported. The OVON and R2R-CE evaluations use authors-chosen short-horizon subsets while baseline numbers come from the full splits, so the comparisons are not like-for-like. No uncertainty is reported. HM3D-IIN and the ablations use ground-truth visual goals and correctly bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling sweep or comparison of representation alignment across model sizes, capabilities, architectures, or training objectives.
No measurement of paired image-caption representation alignment across models of varying performance or scale.
No comparison of models trained from different initializations, shared subspaces, or features across seeds.

Tests one blind-matching approach without paired data through downstream navigation outcomes, but reports no direct representation-mapping error or loss relative to a paired/supervised mapping. It does not test linear maps, stitching, or other interchangeability methods.
No comparison of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits across models.
No comparison of cross-model convergence under alternative representation-similarity measures, settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether alignment plateaus or whether shared data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, explain it.

rows.subject: PlatonicNav (Ours)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate navigation with language goals grounded into a vision-built map by blind matching, without paired vision-language data.
rows.baseline: Various cross-modal ObjNav methods in Table 1; no single baseline stated.
rows.note: The paper reports this as PlatonicNav's Val-Seen OVON result.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with other navigation methods. Success rate mixes segmentation, geometry, planning and the controller, and no blind-matching accuracy or random-label control is reported, so it cannot show V4's mapping quality.
